---
title: "Amortised Analysis: Total Movement, Not Nested Loops"
description: "Memorisable mathematical reasoning with small numerical examples."
---

## When to recognise the pattern

When code contains a while loop nested inside a for loop but each pointer only moves forward.

## The key question

**How can two nested loops still take linear time?**

## Formula worth memorising

$$
\sum_{t=1}^{m}\Delta r_t\le n
$$

**Every symbol explained:** r is a right pointer; Δr_t is how many positions it advances during outer iteration t; m is the number of outer iterations and n is the array length. Σ sums all pointer movements.

**Substitute actual numbers:** For n=5, a pointer might advance by 3, then 1, then 0, then 1, then 0 positions. The total is 3+1+0+1+0=5, not 5 moves on every iteration.

## Why this is mathematically correct

A monotone pointer starts at 0 and never decreases, so across the entire algorithm it can advance at most n positions. Charging each increment once bounds the total inner-loop work by O(n) even though it is syntactically nested.

## Limits and counterexamples

If the inner pointer resets to zero on every outer iteration, the bound no longer holds. Likewise, expensive operations inside an increment can add costs beyond simple O(1) movements.

## The 20-second memory card

**Memorise: Count total pointer increments across the whole run, not the apparent nested-loop shape.**

Now reproduce the equation, example and proof aloud, without looking.

**Interview problems:** Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters; Sliding Window.
